docs.title: openball: every workflow, walked in a real browser
docs.text:
These pages describe what a person does in openball, one page per workflow, with a flow chart, the steps as a story, the screenshot of each step (taken by actually running the app, never drawn), what you should see, and what happens in the edge cases. They are written for testers, owners and anyone who needs to know what the app does, not how it is built.

Start with the case catalogue: every case we check, for every kind of person, and how. To see how the tests sign in (and why there is no back door): LOGIN.md.

docs.title: Case catalogue: every workflow, and every case of it
docs.text:
This is the list of what a person can do in openball and what can go wrong while they do it, for six kinds of people: the anonymous visitor, the player, the group organiser, the team captain (and member), the venue owner and the platform admin. Each case is one thing worth checking, with what should happen, and how it is checked.

How to read the last column:

  • Automated: X1 the case is walked by a journey of the evidence walkthrough (the journey tests). The journey has its own page with pictures: journeys/. It is run in a real browser, on a fresh local stack, and the recorded run is in the docs.
  • Written before #606 was merged. Organised open games and the team name/crest edit (pull request #606) were not on main when these journeys (E1, E2) were written, so they were written against the branch, run green on a stack built from it, and made to skip themselves with a reason on a build without the feature (they ask the running app). #606 has since been merged, so they now run as part of every full run.
  • Finding the case is walked by a journey, and the journey ends in a product problem that is filed as a GitHub issue (linked in the row). The step is recorded as failing in the run on purpose; the case counts as automated in the totals. These labels describe main today (some of those issues are being fixed in other pull requests).
  • Not automatable here and why. These cases are still worth a person's eyes; the reason says what is missing (a real bank, a real inbox, a physical phone, a week of waiting) and, where there is one, which other test proves the rule.

Every journey runs in Greek (the default), and the cases about language also in English. "Light and dark" and "phone width (390 px)" pictures are taken in the same journey where the case is about them.

Totals are at the end of this page (Counts).

The rule (decided by the founders, recorded in issue #602): an open game is organised by a named group of at least one full side (5, 6 or 8), and each member holds their own seat. docs.title: How tests sign in (and why there is no back door)
docs.text: Short version. The tests sign in the way a person does: they ask for a six-digit code and type it. On the local test stack the code is shown on the page (because that stack has no mail server). On the deployed demo, which mails its codes and never returns them, the tests sign in only throwaway @seed.openball.test accounts, and the code is prepared on the server by a test mechanism, then typed on the real sign-in page. There is no special "test login", no password, no hidden address, no inbox and no switch in the product that lets anyone in without a code. Nothing was added to the app for testing.

docs.title: The demo
docs.text: On the demo, the tests sign in only throwaway @seed.openball.test accounts, through a server-side test mechanism that prepares the one-time code for that account. The code is then typed on the real sign-in page, and the real API checks it and creates the session. No back door exists in the product: the sign-in request, the code check and the session are the product's own, and nothing was added to the app for testing. The first sign-in of an address creates the account; the test finishes it through the API's own profile update, and the session is signed out when the test ends. The sign-in code is never mailed, never written to a log, and never visible in a picture. Any address that is not a seed address is refused.

docs.title: Why this cannot become a way into production
docs.text: The product has no test login or bypass. Test accounts sign in through the normal sign-in flow; on the demo a server-side test mechanism supplies their code. This is verified by automated checks, and screenshots and reports never hold a code.

docs.title: Cases that exercise sign-in itself
docs.text: See L1 · Signing in and out: wrong code, five wrong tries, expired code, rate limit, sign-out, expired session. Two of those need time to pass (a code lives ten minutes, a session thirty days). The tests do not wait: a clearly labelled test helper moves the clock of that one row in the local database (the test helpers), and the real API then refuses it exactly as it would after the wait.

docs.title: What is still unproven
docs.text:
• Signing in on the demo through the server-side test mechanism. The whole path (browser, one-time code, real session, profile update, sign-out) is proven on a throwaway local stack, but the production API's behaviour for a seed address (no code in the answer, the real mailer) has not been exercised by this harness yet.
  • The sign-in e-mail reaching a real inbox (no test reads one any more).
  • Sign in with Google (needs a configured Google client) and by SMS (no provider exists).

docs.title: What this flow is for
docs.text:
An open game is a game that already exists (a pitch is held for it) and has free seats; anyone can take one. Taking a seat holds the price on the player's card but does not charge it. The game needs a minimum number of players by the cutoff. At the cutoff the system decides:

  • enough players: the game is ON, every held seat is charged;
  • not enough: the game is cancelled, every hold is released, nobody is charged.

This is the money moment of the whole open-game product, so the journey does not stop at «a seat was held»: it brings the cutoff forward (a labelled test helper moves the clock of that one game; the stack's real worker then decides) and checks the database and Stripe for what happened.

docs.title: What this flow is for
docs.text: The profile is what other players see (a first name, a position, a level, a neighbourhood) and where the player controls their own data: language, light/dark, and, at the end, deleting the account. This journey changes each of those and proves the changes stick, that a cancelled edit leaves nothing behind, and that deleting the account really ends access.

docs.title: The flow at a glance
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Profile] --> B[Edit profile]
    B --> C{Save or cancel?}
    C -->|Save| D[Profile shows name, position,<br/>level, area]
    C -->|Cancel| E[Nothing is kept]
    B --> F[Language: English]
    F --> G[Profile opens in English<br/>notifications will be English]
    A --> H[Appearance switch<br/>Light or Dark]
    H --> H1[Header button agrees]
    A --> I[Delete account]
    I --> J[Page lists what is erased<br/>and what is kept, and why]
    J --> K[Request deletion]
    K --> L[Signed out on every device]
    L --> M[Signing in with that address:<br/>«This account is closed»<br/>with the erasure date]

docs.title: Step by step (from the recorded run)
docs.text:
Step 1. A player who has just joined signs in. Their profile was filled in when they signed up.

on screen: a new player signs in

Step 2. The profile shows their name, position, level and neighbourhood, and «Your record on the pitch»: games played, bookings, times they left, all zero so far, with a sentence explaining that zeros do not mean a lost appearance. At the side: appearance (light/dark), «Register your business», language, accessibility, data sources, delete account, and who they are signed in as.

on screen: they open their profile from the menu

Same moment, in the dark theme and on a phone (390 px):

Step 3. In «Edit profile» they type a new first name (only the first name is asked for, never a surname), add «Forward» to the positions they play, choose the level «Advanced» and change the neighbourhood. Date of birth and e-mail are shown but cannot be changed here, and the page says why.

on screen: they change their name, position, level and area

Same moment, on a phone (390 px):

Step 4. They press «Save». The profile now says Στέλιος, Advanced, Καισαριανή.

on screen: they save and the profile shows the change

Step 5. They start typing a different name and then press «Cancel». The profile still says Στέλιος: a cancelled edit leaves nothing behind.

on screen: an edit that is cancelled is not kept

Step 6. In «Language» they choose English and save. The profile opens in English straight away (the e-mails and notifications they get will be in English too), and it keeps their Greek first name.

on screen: they choose English for notifications and pages

Step 7. On the profile the «Appearance» switch (Light | Dark) shows which is on. Pressing «Dark» turns the page dark and the moon in the header turns into a sun: the two controls always agree.

on screen: the profile has its own light/dark switch

Step 8. From the profile's side menu they open «Delete account». The page lists, in plain words, what is erased (name, e-mail, phone, date of birth, profile, reliability score, every active session) and what is kept and why (bookings and payments without the name, because tax law requires the accounts; anonymous past seats; team memberships without the name), and says it cannot be undone.

on screen: they read what deleting the account would do

Step 9. They press «Request deletion». The account stops working at once and they are signed out of every device; opening the profile now only asks them to sign in.

on screen: they ask for the deletion and are signed out everywhere

Step 10. If they try to come back with the same e-mail address and the right code, they are not let in. A page says «This account is closed» with the date it was closed and the date its data will be erased (30 days later), and offers «Home» and «Sign in with another account», rather than silently making a new account or showing a vague error.

on screen: signing in again with that address is refused, with a sentence that says why

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
• The profile shows a record on the pitch with zeros explained («zeros do not mean a lost appearance»).
  • Only the first name is asked for; date of birth and e-mail are shown but cannot be changed here, with the reason.
  • Saving changes the profile at once; cancelling changes nothing.
  • Choosing English changes the language of the pages and, from then on, of the e-mails and notifications.
  • Deleting is explained before it is asked for: what is erased (name, e-mail, phone, date of birth, profile, reliability score, sessions) and what stays and why (accounting records without the name, anonymous past seats, team memberships without the name). It cannot be undone.
  • Afterwards the same address cannot get in: the page says the account is closed, on which date, and when its data goes.

docs.title: What this flow is for
docs.text: A player wants a pitch or a game near them. The search starts from the ten nearest, shows a photo and a distance for each, and puts the same venues on a map. Filters exist but are optional and closed by default. Where «near» starts comes from, in this order: the device location if they press «Use my location», the postcode in their profile, the area in their profile, and for a visitor the centre of Athens.

    B -->|player with an area| D[10 nearest their area]

docs.title: Step by step (from the recorded run)
docs.text:
Step 1. Someone with no account opens the home page and taps «Pitch search». Without knowing where they are, the page lists the ten pitches nearest the centre of Athens.

on screen: a visitor with no account looks for a pitch: the 10 nearest the centre of Athens

Same moment, on a phone (390 px):

Step 2. A new player signs in. Their profile says they live in Νέα Σμύρνη.

on screen: they sign in as a player living in Νέα Σμύρνη

Step 3. The page now says «The 10 nearest to Νέα Σμύρνη». Each card has a photo (marked «SAMPLE» because they are stock pictures), the pitch, the format, how far away it is (0,3 km, 2,2 km, 2,6 km … growing), the time and the price for the whole pitch.

on screen: the pitch search now starts from their area, nearest first, with photos

Same moment, in the dark theme and on a phone (390 px):

Step 4. Beside the list is a map with a pin per result («10 pitches on the map»), zoom buttons and quick jumps to Centre, South suburbs, West, North and Piraeus. «Show all pitches» zooms back out.

on screen: the map shows the same ten pitches and can jump between areas

Step 5. At the bottom is «More results». It shows the next ten, still ordered by distance, starting where the first ten ended.

on screen: they load the next ten

Step 6. Under «Filters» (closed by default, all optional) they choose the format 6x6 and press «Search». The list narrows to pitches that have 6x6 free. «Clear filters» is always there.

on screen: they narrow it down with the optional filters

Step 7. They search by a pitch name that does not exist. The page does not just go blank: it says «No pitch found», says what it looked for, and offers three ways on: loosen the filters, create your own game, or declare when you are free.

on screen: a filter that matches nothing says so and offers a way out

Step 8. On the pitch search they press «Use my location» and allow the browser to share it. The page reloads centred on where they are («The 10 nearest to your position»). The address keeps the position rounded to about a kilometre, never the exact spot.

on screen: they press «Use my location»

Step 9. The games search says «Find a game with free seats» and, above the list, offers the two ways to start a game of your own (share the cost with a group, or one person pays). When there are open games the list says how it is sorted («first the ones that are nearly full, then the nearest») and that in an open game everyone joins on their own seat, so no group size is checked.

on screen: the games list explains its order and the open-game rule

Same moment, in the dark theme and on a phone (390 px):

Step 10. In «Edit profile» there is an optional postcode field («We only use it to show you nearby games; nobody else sees it»). They type just «12» and press Save: the page refuses an incomplete postcode and says why.

on screen: they add their postcode in the profile

Step 11. They replace it with 18534 (Piraeus) and save. The pitch search now says «The 10 nearest to Πειραιάς» and the Piraeus pitches come first: the postcode, not the old neighbourhood, decides what «near» means.

on screen: a real Piraeus postcode moves the starting point of every search

Step 12. From the footer link «Data sources and licences» they reach a page that names OpenStreetMap, the open licence (ODbL) behind the map and the postcode table, and links to the credit.

on screen: the licences page credits the map data

Same moment, on a phone (390 px):

docs.title: What this flow is for
docs.text: A team is just «your own players with a name». The captain makes it, sends an invite code, and then sets who starts, where, and who sits on the bench, on a pitch picture instead of a form. The saved line-up is what the team later brings into a game. This journey does it all with mouse and taps, including the awkward bits.

Step 1. Maria, who plays five-a-side every week, signs in. Nobody has made a team yet.

on screen: Maria signs in

Step 2. Maria opens «My teams» from the menu. It says she is in no team yet and offers to make one or join one.

on screen: Maria opens «Οι ομάδες μου» and finds it empty

Same moment, on a phone (390 px):

Step 3. She taps «Make a team». The button stays grey until she types a name; as she types, a crest is drawn from the name. She picks the shield shape.

on screen: Maria types a team name and watches the badge appear

Step 4. She presses «Make a team». The team page opens: she is the only player and the captain, and the line-up board is already there, with five empty spots.

on screen: Maria creates the team and lands on its page

Same moment, in the dark theme and on a phone (390 px):

Step 5. Lower on the page is a six-character invite code with «Copy». She sends it to her friends.

on screen: Maria reads the invite code

Step 6. Eight friends enter the code on their own phones. Maria reloads: the team now has nine players, all of them waiting in «Not in the line-up yet».

on screen: eight friends use the code (TEST HELPER: they join through the same route as «Μπες με κωδικό»)

Step 7. The empty spots on the pitch are greyed out and the «Continue» and «Save» buttons are disabled: she has not chosen anyone yet.

on screen: the board is locked until a player is picked

Step 8. She taps her own card and then the goalkeeper spot. Maria is in goal, the counter reads 1 of 5, and a note says there are unsaved changes.

on screen: Maria taps herself, then the goalkeeper spot

Step 9. She presses on Νίκος's card, drags it across the pitch and lets go on a defender spot. He takes the place; the counter reads 2 of 5.

on screen: Maria drags Νίκος onto the first defender spot

Step 10. She tries another shape: «2-2». The pitch redraws with two defenders and two attackers; the players already placed keep their places.

on screen: Maria changes the formation to 2-2

Same moment, in the dark theme:

Step 11. Tired of dragging, she presses «Auto-arrange». The board fills all five spots with the players she has, and the checklist ticks «5 starters on the pitch».

on screen: Maria lets «Αυτόματη τοποθέτηση» fill the rest

Step 12. Straight after dragging, she taps a starter to pick it up for a swap. The card should light up as selected. ⚠️ failed in the recorded run

on screen: Maria taps a starter right after her drag

the first tap after a drag selects the card · expect(locator).toHaveAttribute(expected) failed · Locator: getByRole('button', { name: 'Νίκος, Αμυντικός', exact: true }) · Expected: "true"

Step 13. To swap two people she taps one starter and then another. They trade places, and a hidden announcement tells screen-reader users what moved.

on screen: Maria swaps two players by tapping them one after the other

Step 14. She sends three more friends to the bench. The substitutes box now reads 3 of 3: a team can have at most three substitutes, and they are not charged.

on screen: Maria puts a player on the bench, and the bench has a limit of three

Step 15. She presses «Save line-up». It says «Line-up saved», the checklist is all green, and «Continue with this line-up» lights up for when she books a pitch.

on screen: Maria saves the line-up

Same moment, in the dark theme and on a phone (390 px):

Step 16. She leaves the page and returns later. The line-up is exactly as she saved it.

on screen: the line-up is still there after leaving and coming back

Step 17. At the top of the team page two shortcuts: «Invite players» (back to the code) and «Find an opponent» (the list of teams looking for a match).

on screen: the team hub offers the next moves: invite players, find an opponent

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
• Before any player is picked the spots are greyed out and «Save» and «Continue with this line-up» are disabled.
  • Tapping a player and then a spot (or dragging) puts the player there; the counter reads «Starters 1/5» and a bar says there are unsaved changes (with «Discard» and «Save line-up»).
  • Changing the formation redraws the pitch; auto-arrange fills the empty spots using the players' preferred positions.
  • Tapping two starters in turn swaps them; a hidden live region announces the move to screen-reader users.
  • The bench holds three; the ninth player stays under «Not in the line-up yet».
  • After saving: «Line-up saved», the readiness checklist is complete («5 starters», «You are in the starting line-up», «Line-up saved») and «Continue with this line-up» is enabled. It persists across visits.

docs.title: What this flow is for
docs.text: A team page holds the line-up, an invite code and a list of players, and that is not for everyone. This journey puts three people at the same team and checks what each of them can and cannot do: entering the code (wrongly, then rightly), the read-only view of a plain member, the refusal of a stranger, handing over the captain's armband, a member leaving, and the last captain not being able to walk out.

docs.title: What this flow is for
docs.text: A captain wants to know, first, what needs their answer, and then what their team has coming up. The «Team games» screen puts the challenges other teams sent at the top, each answerable with one press, and below it a timeline of the team's matches by day, each with a state in words and an icon. The same events arrive as notifications, and the sender is told when a challenge is turned down.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
• Answer-first. The first block is the invitations («3 waiting for an answer»); each card names the challenger, the pitch, the day and time, an optional message from them, her half of the price, and two actions: accept (with the amount) or «No thanks». A countdown in words («in 33 hours», «tomorrow») says how long she has to answer.
  • My matches, by day. Each match shows the two crests (a dashed circle with «Find an opponent» when the second team is missing), the pitch and time, the price of her half, and a state that is always a word plus an icon: Deposit missing, Waiting for a second team, Booked.
  • Notifications. One unread row per challenge; marking one read lowers the counter; the challenger receives a row when a challenge is declined.
  • Teams looking for an opponent. The public matches of other teams.

docs.title: How the matches get there (a note for testers)
docs.text: Nothing in the screens can create one of these legacy team matches today (the create route is retired), so the journey starts with a clearly labelled test preparation step: the repository's own sample-data seed (the seed data script) is run against the test stack. It creates the account's team and ten players who join with a real invite code, saves a line-up, creates the matches and has demo teams challenge Maria's. The seed is guarded: it only runs against the walkthrough's own local database (the test helpers).

docs.title: What this flow is for
docs.text: First impressions. Before anyone has an account they should understand what openball is, be able to read it in their language, in light or dark, on a phone, and with a keyboard alone; reach the information pages; and when they try to book they should be asked to sign in, not thrown an error. It also covers the header light/dark button added in #601.

docs.title: Step by step (from the recorded run)
docs.text:
Step 1. Someone opens openball for the first time. The page says what it is for in one line, offers the two ways in («Find a game» and «Find a pitch»), shows one open game they could join right now with its price, and explains how the money works.

on screen: a visitor opens the home page

Same moment, in the dark theme and on a phone (390 px):

Step 2. In the header is a small moon button (its label says «Appearance: Dark»). They press it and the whole page turns dark; the button becomes a sun that offers the way back.

on screen: they switch the page to dark with the toggle in the header

Step 3. They go to the pitch search and reload it: it stays dark. They press the sun and it is light again. The choice belongs to this browser; nothing is sent to the server.

on screen: the dark choice is remembered on the next page and after a reload

Step 4. The header has an EL | EN switch. They press EN and the same page appears in English: heading, buttons, prices and dates follow. The address changes from /el to /en.

on screen: they switch to English

Same moment, in the dark theme:

Step 5. Inside the English site, the next pages are English too, and the EL link in the header leads to the same page in Greek, not back to the home page.

on screen: the English page keeps them in English as they move around

Step 6. At the width of a phone (390 px) the layout is a single column with a tab bar at the bottom (Home, Pitches, Games, Bookings, Profile) and nothing scrolls sideways.

on screen: on a phone the same site has a tab bar

Step 7. Under «How the money works» on the home page is a link to a longer explanation: a seat is held (not charged) until the game is certain, and released in full if it is not.

on screen: they read how the money works

Step 8. A pitch owner who lands here taps «Sign in as a pitch owner». They are taken to a sign-in page that is worded for owners, and after signing in they would continue to registering their business.

on screen: they look at the page for pitch owners

Step 9. At the bottom of every page are the accessibility statement, an explanation of how results are ranked, and the data sources and licences. Each one opens a real page.

on screen: the footer legal pages open

Step 10. Someone who uses only the keyboard presses Tab once on the home page. A «Skip to content» link appears first, and Enter jumps over the menu to the main part of the page.

on screen: with the keyboard alone: the first Tab offers «Skip to content»

Step 11. A friend has sent a team code. From the home page they tap «Join a team with a code». They are not signed in, so the page says «You need an account to join the team — one step; when you are signed in we bring you back here to type the code», with a sign-in button that remembers the way back.

on screen: a visitor with a team code is asked to sign in first

Step 12. A mistyped address shows «We could not find this page. The link may be wrong or the page may have moved», with two ways on: «Find a pitch» and «Home page».

on screen: a page that does not exist says so kindly

Same moment, on a phone (390 px):

Step 13. They open a free pitch hour from the search. The page shows the whole offer (day, time, price and the two ways to start a game) and the button «Gather your group» is a sign-in link: it leads to sign-in, and the address remembers which hour they wanted.

on screen: booking without an account asks them to sign in first

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
• The home page says in one line what it is for, offers Find a game and Find a pitch, shows an open game with its price per player when one is open, and explains that a seat is held, not charged until the game is certain.
  • The moon button in the header turns the whole page dark; the button then shows a sun. The choice survives moving between pages and reloading (it is stored in this browser only).
  • Pressing EN shows the same page in English and the address changes from /el to /en; the EL link on an English page returns to the same page in Greek.
  • At 390 px there is one column, a bottom tab bar (Home, Pitches, Games, Bookings, Profile) and no horizontal scrolling.
  • A mistyped address shows a friendly 404 with «Find a pitch» and «Home page».

docs.title: What this flow is for
docs.text: Some pages are not for everyone: the platform admin screens, the owner's console, the notifications, the team games. The rule for every one of them is the same: a refusal is a plain sentence and a way on, never a crash, and never a hint of what is behind the door. This journey tries the doors with the keys people actually have.

docs.title: Step by step (from the recorded run)
docs.text:
Step 1. A visitor types the address of the platform admin page. They are not shown anything: they are sent to the sign-in page, which remembers where they were headed.

on screen: a visitor with no account tries the admin pages

Step 2. Trying a page of the owner console sends them to an owner-worded sign-in («Owner sign-in: we send a code to your e-mail and you continue to your pitch console»).

on screen: the same visitor tries the owner console

Same moment, on a phone (390 px):

Step 3. The notifications page says «Sign in to see your notifications — they are personal and only appear once you are signed in». «Team games» says «You need an account to continue». Neither shows anyone else's data.

on screen: and the notifications and team games, which are personal

Step 4. Dimitra signs in. She is a player: she has no business and no admin rights.

on screen: a plain player signs in

Step 5. She opens the admin page: «You do not have access here. This section is only for people who run the platform. If you think you should have access, ask …». The same for the money-reconciliation page. There is no data behind the message.

on screen: the admin pages refuse a player in plain words

Same moment, on a phone (390 px):

Step 6. She opens the owner console («Today»). Having no business, she is told that to put pitches and hours on openball she first needs a business, which takes two minutes, with a button to register one. Bookings and earnings say the same: there is nothing of anyone else's here.

on screen: the owner console offers a player to register a business, and shows nothing else

Step 7. Meanwhile the venue owner (in their own browser) sees their venues in the console. When they try the admin page they get the same «You do not have access here»: being an owner does not make anyone an admin.

on screen: the owner's own console opens for the owner

Step 8. Dimitra gets hold of the address of one of that owner's venue pages and opens it. She sees «We could not find this page» (a 404, the same as for an address that never existed), so nothing reveals that the venue exists or what is in it.

on screen: a player who knows the address of that owner's venue gets «not found»

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
• The refusal for a signed-in non-admin on an admin page is a page («You do not have access here. This section is only for people who run the platform. If you think you should have access, ask …»), not an error, and shows no data.
  • A player opening the owner console is not shown a broken page: they are offered to register a business.
  • A venue address that is not yours behaves exactly as an address that does not exist (404), so it cannot be used to find out which venues exist or what is in them.

docs.text: • A second owner against the first: it needs a second fully approved business (the onboarding is in O1). The same refusal is shown for a non-staff account here, and the staff check is proven in the API tests (an automated API test).

docs.title: X1 · The link crawler
docs.text: Who Four robots: a visitor, a player, an owner and an admin, each in Greek and English Test id X1 (four tests, one per kind of person) Needs the local stack Catalogue V-14, X-01 in CATALOGUE.md

docs.title: What this flow is for
docs.text:
A person only needs one dead end to lose trust. The crawler starts where each kind of person starts and follows every link it can reach (and every button that only opens more; locally also every plain button that navigates), in Greek and in English. On every page it checks for: a 404, a «coming soon» stub, a server error, a raw translation key, undefined or NaN on screen, a disabled main button with no explanation, and any console error or failed request.

It cannot write. For the whole crawl every request to the app that is not a read is aborted and listed («would have written…»), and a second line of defence never presses a button whose name says it acts (pay, cancel, book, delete…). The run then checks the app's own request log: a crawl that caused any write fails.

docs.title: The flow at a glance
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S[Start pages of one kind of person] --> L[Follow every same-site link]
    L --> G{Dead-end guard<br/>and client-error check}
    G -->|clean| N[Next page]
    G -->|404, stub, error, raw key,<br/>console error| R[Row in the report:<br/>page, link that led there,<br/>picture]
    N --> L
    L --> W[Writes are blocked and listed]

docs.text: The summary lists every page visited (one picture each), the Dead ends and failed pages table (empty means none) and the Writes the crawler blocked table. A full crawl visits hundreds of pages, so this page shows only the first few as a sample; the complete set is in the run's report.
